Executive Summary
This project presents the design and implementation of the DiabetesCare Platform across two distinct architectural stages, each aligned with specific cloud computing objectives. The progression from a monolithic deployment to a serverless, event-driven architecture demonstrates key principles of scalability, modularity, and operational observability.
In Task 1, the platform is deployed as a monolithic application on a single Amazon EC2 instance. The instance runs Nginx to serve the React frontend and reverse-proxy API requests to a Node.js/Express backend. Amazon RDS PostgreSQL serves as the persistent database, with network isolation enforced through a dedicated VPC and security groups. Access to the database is strictly limited to the application layer, ensuring that only the EC2 instance can communicate with RDS over private network paths.
In Task 2, the platform evolves into a serverless, event-driven architecture designed for production-ready scalability and visibility. The frontend is migrated from EC2 to Amazon S3 for static hosting, with Amazon CloudFront providing global content delivery and HTTPS termination. The backend API is re-architected using Amazon API Gateway (HTTP API) and an AWS Lambda function named ApiFunction, which runs the Express framework inside a VPC to maintain secure connectivity to RDS. To support asynchronous microservice-style processing, an admin-triggered workflow is introduced: the API sends job messages to an SQS queue, which are consumed by a separate worker Lambda, SqsSummaryWorker. This worker generates JSON artifacts stored in an S3 Reports bucket and publishes completion notifications through an SNS topic. Observability is enhanced across both Lambda functions with CloudWatch Logs, a CloudWatch Alarm to monitor API function errors, and AWS X-Ray for distributed tracing. Collectively, Task 2 achieves improved modularity, operational visibility, and scalability while fulfilling the required integration, monitoring, and event-driven architecture deliverables.



Task 1: Basic Architecture (Monolithic EC2 + RDS PostgreSQL)
The Diabetic Care Platform is launched in an independent Virtual Private cloud (VPC) called diabetic-care-vpc whose CIDR block is 10.0.0.0/20. In order to implement a strong security boundary, this VPC will be divided into two separate tiers: web facing components will be implemented in public subnets and sensitive data storage will be implemented in private subnets. Public level will include diabetic-care-subnet-public1-us-east-1a (10.0.0.0/24) and diabetic-care-subnet-public2-us-east-1b (10.0.1.0/24). The database is separated into the private data tier (isolated in diabetic-care-subnet-private1-us-east-1a (10.0.8.0/24) and diabetic-care-subnet-private2-us-east-1b (10.0.9.0/24).
The whole application stack is monolithic on a single EC2 instance called diabetic-care-server. This example contains Nginx that has two main purposes in serving the react frontend that is static and a reverse proxy that delivers API traffic. The frontend application is provided directly as the /var/www/diabetic-care/frontend/dist and, at the same time, Nginx is set to receive the requests addressed to the /api/ route and redirect it to the local backend application on http/localhost:3001/api/.
It has a backend composed of a Node.js/Express API deployed with PM2 and listening on port one thousand three hundred. It has been based on Prisma as an Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) tool to manage all the database operations. The database layer is a database Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database named diabetic-care-database that is located in the private subnets so as not to be exposed to the internet.
Security groups are used to provide security at the network level. The RDS case is linked to a security group called diabetic-care-rds-sg which has one inbound rule that allows TCP traffic over port 5432. This is strictly applied to all traffic that comes out of the security group of the EC2 instance, diabetic-care-web-sg. This setup will ensure that only the application server can access the database and this will serve to protect the integrity of data and ensure that it is not accessed by unauthorized external users.

Task 2: Sophisticated Serverless Single-AZ Architecture (Event-driven)
The improved Diabetic Care Platform takes the form of serverless architecture to specify system scalability and visibility in the operation but retains its essence. The frontend called React is served in a private S3 bucket in Amazon and distributed across the world using Amazon CloudFront that utilizes the https to prevent terminal and content delivery. The application is accessed by the users through the Cloudfront URL which is secure in providing the contents of S3 origin as static content.
The API is implemented on Amazon API Gateway which is an HTTP API and all the requests are redirected to a Lambda function named ApiFunction at the backend. In order to access the Amanda RDS PostgreSQL database in a safe way, the ApiFunction Lambda will be deployed in the VPC which will allow Prisma to connect to databases using the private network.
The architecture is proposed to be an event-driven and asynchronous pipeline of microservice to facilitate workloads which are initiated by the administration. For an administrator to call the POST /api/ integrations/ async- summary endpoint, the ApiFunction will create a job message to SQS queue called AsyncJobsQueue. This queue calls another inventory worker Lambda called SqsSummaryWorker that finishes the job of creating a summary artifact execution of quantum data to a S3 object storage, called ReportsBucket using a PutObject action. When it is successfully done, the worker sends notification to an SNS topic named NotificationTopic under the Publish operation and it lets the downstream subscribers to respond to the event.
The architecture has operational observability which makes it easy to monitor and troubleshoot. Both Lambda automatically publish runtime logs to CloudWatch logs where they can provide execution history in detail. AWS X-Ray tracing is also enabled to trace end-to-end request flows through API Gateway and Lambda to downstream AWS services to help do performance analysis and debugging. There is also a CloudWatch Alarm which is set to watch error metrics of the ApiFunction in particular to enable the operations team to be alerted when there are API-Level failures.

Changes from Task 1 to Task 2
The Diabetic Care Platform initially took the form of a monolithic application that would be deployed as a single EC2 instance. Nginx was used for the React frontend and reverse-proxed all API traffic to an Express backend that connected directly to the RDS. While working, this architecture faced some limitations in terms of scalability, visibility of operations and the ability to efficiently process asynchronous workload. Task 2 overcomes these limitations by adapting the platform to a production-ready, serverless architecture, decomposing it into more distinct components, implementing an event-driven processing, and configuring solid observability practices.
Organizing transformation is organized around three core improvements:
Frontend hosting and delivery - The frontend of React is now moved from being served on EC2/Nginx static to a serverless hosting model using an S3 private bucket as the origin, and it is served using CloudFront, which provides global content delivery, provides an https termination, and enhances its performance.
Backend API modernization - The express based monolithic backend is replaced with a serverless API layer consisting of API Gateway (HTTP API) which routes all requests to a Lambda function named ApiFunction. This function is which runs the Express framework inside Lambda and connecting safely to RDS PostgreSQL from within the VPC using Prisma.
Asynchronous microservice processing - An event-driven pipeline is introduced that handle the workload initiated by admin. The ApiFunction sends job messages to SQS queue, which will send a special Lambda function (SqsSummaryWorker) that will be bound to this event. This job will work on the jobs by writing summaries in the form of a combination of these two items to an S3 reports bucket and by publishing notifications from an SNS topic, decoupling this long running operation from the main API flow. Observability is standardized on both Lambda functions using CloudWatch Logs for logging and X-Ray for distributed tracing and a CloudWatch Alarm to monitor the errors on the ApiFunction.

Serverless Components Implementation 
Amazon VPC & Security Groups
The Diabetic Care Platform is launched in a special VPC called diabetic-care-vpc and has a CIDR block of 10.0.0.0/20 divided by two Availability Zones. Public subnets of (10.0.0.0/24 and 10.0.1.0/24) are hosting web-tier resources and private subnets of (10.0.8.0/24 and 10.0.9.0/24) are isolating RDS db and VPC bound Lambda functions.
Security groups implement network access control. The Lambda security group controls the outbound traffic from the Lambda ENIs, while the RDS security group grants the inbound TCP traffic on port 5432 access from the Lambda security group. Some of the key points of using the VPC are: - This setup provides private connectivity between the backend and database while restricting access to the RDS instance.








2.1 Amazon RDS (Relational Database Service)
The platform has Amazon RDS (PostgreSQL) as the long-term relational data store. RDS works out by providing managed backups, patching and availability without having to deal with the administration of the database engine directly.
The backend (Prisma ORM) makes the connection with RDS via a DATABASE_URL, set for API Lambda. RDS security group is set to permit only inbound PostgreSQL traffic (TCP 5432) by the Lambda security group (principle of least privilege), so that the access to the database was not open to the rest of the world. 









Amazon S3 (Storage Worker + Frontend Hosting)

The Diabetic Care Platform has two different uses of Amazon S3 to store, which are asynchronous processing to the backend and delivery to the front end. For backend operations it uses a special dedicated bucket for artifacts generated by asynchronous worker pipeline i.e. ReportsBucket. Once the SqsSummaryWorker receives a job on the SQS queue, it uploads the results of summary jobs triggered by an administrator to this bucket using PutObject operation and makes the output of summary jobs long-lasting.
For frontend delivery, a static website is hosted on a separate S3 bucket where the React user interface is hosted on. Instead of hosting the content in S3, the service utilizes to a content delivery network of Amazon CloudFront to spread the frontend to the rest of the world with low latency and inbuilt HTTPS functionality. The frontend application is set up with VITEAPIURL environment variable that is configured to the deployed Http API gateway base URL allowing the React application to safely forward the authenticated API requests to the back-end services.



2.8 Amazon CloudFront (CDN for Frontend)
The frontend of the React-based S3 hosted application is served by CloudFront deriving onto a speedier platform with lower latency. Frontend will be requested through CloudFront HTTPS domain and API calls will be performed directly to API Gateway URL used in VITEAPIURL.

Performance Analysis 
Based on the evidence collected in the monitoring by Amazon CloudWatch, including Lambda logs and metrics and the alarm set up for alarm notification, in addition to the benefit of visibility to traces by AWS X-Ray, the Diabetic Care Platform showed predictable good performance characteristics from the integration of Task 2. The serverless architecture makes scaling effective as the heart of the backend is, in turn, managed by AWS lambda running behind API gateway. When the load is normal and the requests are parallel, the Lambda will automatically scale up to additional concurrent executions without the need to scale and manage the server or instances manually. This results in better responsiveness than the monolithic approach to EC2 that we used in task 1 and is much less of a burden operationally than.
There is further benefit to the system due to decoupled asynchronous processing. Admin triggered summary jobs are queued from the API Lambda to Amazon Squad and then sent to a separate worker lambda, Sqs Summary Worker that will write artifacts to the Report S3 bucket and publish to the SNS. This design separated long running or non critical workloads away from the user facing API path such that temporary delays or retries in workers will not affect authentication work and core API endpoints.
A trade off that is known for Lambda based deployment is cold start latency, which could happen when functions are idle and are called once after some inactivity. This may result in a observable delay in the response time on the first request following an idle period in our deployment, with subsequent requests generally executing more quickly as a result of warm execution environments. In a production scenario, measures can be implemented to mitigate cold start impacts: they can be as simple as Provisioned Concurrency, the optimized size of dependencies, and the consideration of runtime configurations.
Overall, Task 2 provides better modularity, as well as scalability and observability than Task 1. With the help of CloudWatch metrics and logs (including the API error alarm) and X-Ray traces, the system becomes more simple to monitor and troubleshoot too. Individual components like the API Lambda and SQS worker can be scaled and analyzed separately keeping true with the best practices of cloud native and building the platform for a perfect future growth.

Conclusion

This project illustrates how the Diabetic Care Platform changed its design of a monolithic cloud deployment (Task 1) to serverless, event-driven architecture, with monitoring (Task 2).
Task 1: In Task 1, the system was deployed as a single-server solution in which the EC2 instance was hosting both the frontend and backend parts, and the backend was directly attached to the RDS PostgreSQL. This solution was easy to implement and generated a bigger operational load and an increased reliance on one compute instance.
AWS managed services were utilized in Task 2, which enhanced the architecture to a larger extent in making it more modular and eliminate the overhead of managing servers. Front end was split into S3 + Cloudfront, and the backend was transferred to API Gateway + Lambda where it has access to the private database. Another feature of the system was an asynchronous microservice workflow based on SQS, specialized worker Lambda, S3 to store generated artifacts, and SNS to receive notifications. The CloudWatch logs, CloudWatch error alarm, and X-Ray tracing were used to monitor requirements.
In general, the Task 2 design offers better principles of cloud-native best practices: observability, scalability, and decoupling. Although serverless comes with the challenges of cold starts and configuration (CORS, caching, environment variables, permissions), the resulting architecture can be considered reliable, simple to scale, and easier to monitor, which meets the coursework objectives and gives a solid basis on creating future improvements.
